splits.remainder: attribute list, the repetition of members
splits.claim: An attribute list is a DECORATION: it adds fields to the node its host built and no node of its own, so a document with the list and the same document without it parse to the same tree modulo those fields, and the difference between what this parser spends on the two is what the list costs IN THAT HOST. The remainder's bytes are identical in every host, so the job is the same in every row -- decode these bytes -- and the reference for it is this parser decoding the same bytes ALONE, through the attribute runner the lexbor comparison uses: `In place / alone` is what the host adds to the list, and it is the composition. What measuring the host without the list (its pair, or its own document) and the list without a host (lexbor) each miss is exactly that seam, and a split of one corpus into a paired part and a bound part would report the local optimum and never the global loss. This table is what stops that: the cost per list is read from two whole documents, over the two stages and over the whole parse path (the second includes releasing what the list built, which the stages do not), so a change that defers the list's work past a stage boundary shows as the gap between the two columns widening, and a change that makes a host cheaper alone while its seam with the list gets dearer shows as the host's `In place / alone` rising while its pair improves. The hosts are the attachment table of docs/specs/dialect/attributes.md, one row per site production, less two the table names and this cannot hold: the bracketed span, whose list is mandatory, so there is no span without one to subtract; and the nameless container, whose opening fence IS the list, so it is the host and not a decoration. Its named form is the container host, and both halves keep the nameless `::: {}` unchanged. Where the grammar admits whitespace before the list -- an ATX heading, which removes the suffix and the whitespace before it; a link reference definition, which requires it -- the host declares that separator and it belongs to the site, not to the list: the audit inserts separator plus bytes, and the marginal contains the separator's scan, which is part of what that site costs. Everywhere else the bytes follow the host with nothing between, because a space before the list is what stops it attaching. Each row names the site production the grammar gives it; the spread between rows is that production first and this implementation's seam second, and the `Lands in` column says which parser this implementation reads the list with, not which the grammar assigns it to. Why this is not the subtraction the README rejects: subtraction drew a boundary INSIDE one measurement, through a call graph that does not carry it. Here the boundary is in the corpus, between two whole documents that differ by exactly the remainder's bytes, every instruction of both is counted, and the audit holds the two trees equal modulo the fields the remainder populates. Second-order effects are in the number rather than hidden by it.

unpairable.proof: RE-DERIVED, because the first statement was the construct-not-production error and happened to survive it. Wrong version: CommonMark has no production that derives a binding from a node's own content. That invites the obvious counter -- a link reference definition also NORMALISES a string and registers it in a name table, which is the same subsequent operation, and it is exactly the reasoning that produced the discarded 1.27x pair. The real difference is in the production, not the operation: a link reference definition IS a binding declaration and builds no block; a derived anchor is a binding attached as a SIDE EFFECT to a block that carries inline content and exists independently of it. Neither reference grammar attaches a derived binding to a content-bearing block, so there is nothing of that shape to write. The former explicit-anchor comparison is also insufficient: its target ownership differs, and the review now measures a declaration/host boundary.

The only proof here with the right SHAPE -- an exhaustive enumeration over both grammars rather than a claim about one construct -- and it is restated as one. An inline footnote is recognised mid-line, its body is parsed as INLINE content, and its node is hoisted out of the content tree into a document-owned side list. Enumerate every inline production of both grammars: code span, emphasis, strong, link, image, autolink, raw HTML, hard break, soft break, entity, text; plus GFM's strikethrough, autolink literal and footnote reference. Every one of them leaves its node where it was recognised. Hoisting exists in GFM only for the footnote DEFINITION, which is a block. So the enumeration is complete and the shape is absent from both grammars. NOTE the honest caveat: nine of the ten claims withdrawn today were single-construct assertions, and this one has not been attacked by anyone but its author.

An exhaustive enumeration over the HOISTING productions of both reference grammars, which is the shape a proof here has to have. An anonymous specimen is an opener owning block content whose node is moved OUT of the content tree into a document-owned side list, with NO name registered. Enumerate every production in CommonMark and GFM that moves something out of the content tree: the link reference definition, which annihilates its source and registers a name; and the GFM footnote definition, which hoists its node and registers a name. That is the complete list -- two -- and BOTH require a non-empty label. Checked rather than asserted: cmark-gfm leaves `[^]: body` as an ordinary paragraph, and CommonMark's label rule requires at least one non-whitespace character, so neither will accept the empty label the anonymous form needs. Dropping the hoist to reach something nameless -- a bullet list item opens a sequence member with no identity and owns block content by indentation -- drops a subsequent operation that the criterion requires to match, and the second clause is not optional. The labelled form has a fresh-key graph proof in specimen-graph-v2, including XML and HTML edge checks; the explicit reset retains its own boundary. Their former counts do not certify arbitrary graph mappings. This enumeration concerns only the nameless-hoist shape. NOTE the honest caveat, the same one the inline footnote carries: this proof has not been attacked by anyone but its author.

unpairable.production: multiline table, the ROW production at two columns or more
unpairable.proof: An exhaustive enumeration over the LINE-CUTTING productions of both reference grammars, and it is narrow on purpose: it concerns the parallel-cut/block-content composition. A multiline row cuts ONE line into K parallel pieces at positions established by one earlier boundary line, appends each piece to its own cell buffer, and parses each buffer as BLOCKS -- checked on the parser, where `- item` in a cell becomes a List and `# Head` becomes a Heading, so it is block parsing and not a joined paragraph. Enumerate every reference production that cuts a line. Every CONTAINER cuts a PREFIX and yields exactly ONE remainder: a block quote strips its marker, a list item strips its content indent, and nesting them cuts the same line repeatedly rather than into parallel pieces. Exactly one reference production cuts a line into K>=2 parallel pieces, GFM's pipe table row, and it parses its pieces as INLINES. So a K-way cut whose pieces are block-parsed exists in neither grammar, and the criterion's second clause -- the subsequent operation must match -- is what the pipe row fails. The one-column reduction that saved the grid table is not available either: a multiline table takes its columns from a SEGMENTED dash line, and a single unbroken dash run is a thematic break or a setext underline. What must NOT be read into this: restricted examples of both factors have reconstructed proof domains: simple-matrix-v2 compares two-column inline cells and grid-cell-v2 compares one block cell. These restricted proofs do not certify their arbitrary composition. It is only their composition that has no reference production. NOTE the honest caveat, the same one the other enumerations carry: this proof has not been attacked by anyone but its author.

unpairable.production: attribute list, the repetition of members
unpairable.proof: An exhaustive enumeration over every production of both reference grammars that reads a DELIMITED MEMBER LIST after or around a construct and decodes it into fields of what that construct builds, and it is narrow on purpose: at one member, the list is paired. An attribute list is a brace-delimited run of REPEATED members, unbounded in number, of three kinds selected by each member's first byte -- `#` an anchor, `.` a class, a name a record with a value in one of three forms (absent, bare, quoted) -- with names the grammar does not know in advance, every member appended in order to the node the host built (attributes.md: classes and records are appended, never deduplicated). The reconstructed class-span-v2 and record-span-v2 domains preserve the class or record key/value with explicit link-field encodings. The old mixed span workload remains diagnostic; restricted proofs do not certify arbitrary attributes. What has no reference production is the REPETITION: an unbounded sequence of members of three kinds, decoded member by member into the same node. Enumerate every reference production that reads a delimited member list. The inline link and the image read `(destination "title")`: two positions, never more, selected by position and never named. The link reference definition reads a label, a destination and a title: three positions. The autolink reads `<destination>` and the fenced code block its info string: one each. GFM's delimiter row reads `| :-- | --: |`: unbounded, but positional over a closed alphabet of four alignments, and a line of its own rather than a suffix of a construct. GFM's footnote reference and definition read a label: one. A character reference decodes one code point; the ordered-list marker, the ATX marker run and GFM's task marker each decode one typed field. Every one of these is fixed in arity or positional over a closed alphabet; none reads a repetition of named members. The one production in either reference grammar that DOES read repeated `name=value` members is the HTML open tag, at two sites: inline raw HTML, and HTML block start condition 7, which requires a complete open tag on the line. At both sites the reference scans the attribute list -- name, optional `=`, bare or quoted value -- to decide that the run is a tag, and then keeps the run as one literal, parsed as a raw HTML tag and rendered without escaping, appending no member to anything: the criterion's second clause, that the subsequent operation must match, is what both sites fail, and a pair written on either would put a list decoded member by member against one that is scanned and kept. The precedents the README lists do not reach it either: the sigil-introduced leaves (the directive, cross-link and embed pairs) pair a construct that BUILDS a node and populates its fields, where the list builds none, so a pair for the list would need a reference production that decorates an existing node with an unbounded member list, and the enumeration finds none. So the repetition is measured two ways and neither is a pair: alone, against lexbor's HTML attribute tokenizer, which does decode the members (`scripts/benchmark-attributes.mjs`); and IN PLACE, inside every site the attachment table admits it at, as a `splits` entry whose reference is this parser decoding the same bytes alone. NOTE the honest caveat, the same one the other enumerations carry: this proof has not been attacked by anyone but its author.

suppressions.rule: a heading as the isomorph half -- CONTAMINATES Grammar and Shape, NOT same-job
suppressions.statement: WITHDRAWN AS STATED, and the correction runs the other way. The claim was that a heading can never be the reference half of a pair anywhere in this corpus, because this dialect derives an anchor on every heading including in plain CommonMark. The premise is true and the conclusion does not follow. Take the three numbers as the driver computes them: grammar = core/twinCore, shape = twinCore/twinCmark, sameJob = core/twinCmark. The anchor derivation lands in twinCore -- this parser's cost on the isomorph half -- and twinCore CANCELS out of sameJob, which is this parser on the DIALECT document over the REFERENCE on the isomorph. The dialect document has no headings and cmark derives no anchors, so sameJob is clean. What is contaminated is Grammar, whose denominator is inflated so it reads low, and Shape, whose numerator is inflated so it reads high. A heading isomorph therefore yields a valid same-job ratio -- the number the ranking sorts on -- and two numbers that must be suppressed.
